compute.reported_as: Sec. III.C.1: Our standard ACE architecture, trained without explicit symmetries, achieves a ground-state energy of −0.76464(1). This result is already more accurate than that of HFPS [23] while requiring only one-fifteenth of the cost. By directly optimizing the projected, symmetrized state reach a new state-of-the-art energy of −0.76623(1). This surpasses the previous best result −0.766073(6) from NNBF [25] with only one-sixth of the computational cost. Additionally, a GFMC calculation with the ACE trial wave-function gives an even lower energy of −0.76647(2). ... Appendix B: In the first stage, we perform 3×10^4 initial steps without enforcing any symmetry. ... First, we restore D2 and spin inversion symmetry and train for 4×10^3 steps. Next, we additionally restore the half-translation symmetries and train for another 4×10^3 steps. Finally, we restore the 1/4-translational symmetries and train for 10^3 steps. ... Table V (Hyperparameters for the MARCH optimizer): Learning rate schedule (t): ACE 10^-1 (1 + max(t−1000,0)/4000)^-1, SCALE 5×10^-1 (1 + max(t−1000,0)/8000)^-1; Optimizer momentum (µ,β) 0.95, 0.995; Damping (λ) 0.001; Batch size clip(32 Lx×Ly, 4096, 8192); Local energy clipping 5.0; MCMC steps per sample 2.5 Lx×Ly; Total optimization steps 50000. Shared parameters apply to both models. ... Table VI (Model hyperparameters): SCALE-S h_conv 256, h_MLP 512, L_conv 1, L_MLP 4; SCALE 512/512/1/4; SCALE-L 384/512/1/4; SCALE-XL 640/1280/1/4 (32×32 only); ACE h_conv 144, h_MLP 256, L_conv 16, L_MLP 2; ACE-L 192/256/16/2. ... Fig. 2 / Sec. III.A: for the largest system size tested (N = 512), SCALE completes an optimization step in approximately 11 seconds. In comparison, the ACE architecture requires about 120 seconds, while the Transformer needs over 400 seconds ... under a fixed batch size. (No hardware named.)

compute.reported_as: Sec. III (Optimizing multi-determinants): As shown in Fig. 3, for the n_h = 2048 model, optimization with four symmetries improves the energy by 29% (43% after full projection), optimization with the 32 symmetries improves the energy by 54% (67% after full projection), and optimization with all 512 symmetries improves the energy by 75% relative to the single MLP ansatz with same n_h. These additional optimizations all use the single-determinant NNBF as a starting point and, in total, take approximately 200, 800, and 3000 GPU hours respectively. [...] The HFPS reaches an energy of -0.76413 which is somewhat higher then the -0.76486(2) of our symmetry optimization with 32 determinants. Additionally, our result can be further projected at essentially no cost to the fully symmetric state to reach an energy of -0.76560(1) [...] The optimization of our 32 determinant MLP-NNBF is faster by approximately a factor of 2 compared with the HFPS. || Sec. II.B: All optimizations reported in this paper were performed using H100 GPUs on GH200 superchips. Most optimizations were performed using a single H100 GPU, but longer optimizations were parallelized across 4 GPUs. GPU times are reported as cumulative GPU usage (e.g. parallelized times are 4 times the wall clock time). All optimization times include the cumulative cost of optimization for a given point which includes (where specified) optimizing smaller ansatz first. || Appendix B: Unless otherwise specified, the total number of markov chains is fixed at N_s = 1024 and the learning rate is fixed at 3 x 10^-4. We first train the single particle orbitals without backflow for 10^5 VMC iterations. [...] The training for the data in Fig. A1 took 3 x 10^6 VMC iterations, followed by 5 x 10^5 VMC iterations with an exponential decay learning rate schedule tuning the learning rate to 10^-7. The training for the model with 4 symmetries took approximately 8 x 10^5 VMC iterations, while the training for the model with 32 symmetries took approximately 5 x 10^5 VMC iterations. || Sec. II.A: Our MLP is fully connected with two hidden layers each followed by a layer normalization and relu activation.
